prompt_free_text:
This paper tackles an important and practically motivated problem: extracting product attributes in an open-world setting with only light supervision. The paper’s central premise is compelling. In realistic e-commerce environments, attribute vocabularies evolve continuously, exhaustive annotation is expensive, and systems that only operate over a fixed ontology are of limited utility. Framing the task as simultaneously expanding known seed attributes and discovering entirely new attribute types is therefore meaningful. The paper also contributes a new dataset and a method, Amacer, that combines seed-supervised contrastive learning with two forms of weak implicit supervision. Overall, I found the paper interesting, timely, and stronger on problem formulation and practical motivation than many prior works in this area. The empirical gains over the chosen baselines are also substantial enough to suggest that the proposed combination of candidate generation, representation learning, and clustering is effective.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the task formulation. The distinction from both closed-world tagging and zero-shot extraction is clearly articulated, and the proposed setting is indeed closer to how product catalogs evolve in practice. The paper also does a good job motivating why titles alone are insufficient and why bullet points matter for open-world discovery. The dataset design appears thoughtful in this respect: including full product horizons rather than only titles is a meaningful step forward. The seed-set construction procedure is also sensible from a practical standpoint. Using retailer-provided profiles, aggressively sanitizing them, and then applying light human curation is a realistic compromise between scalability and quality. This is one of the paper’s most convincing contributions.

Methodologically, the paper is not radically novel in each individual component, but the overall design is coherent and reasonably well matched to the task. The syntax-based candidate generation is simple, but simplicity is a virtue here: it avoids overfitting to the seed set and appears to outperform segmentation-based alternatives in both quality and efficiency. The supervised contrastive objective for seed expansion is standard but appropriate. The adaptive expansion stage is also intuitive and practically useful, especially because it explicitly separates expansion of known attributes from discovery of residual clusters. The most novel part is the use of implicit signals for new attribute discovery: the bullet-point self-supervised heuristic and the latent-attribute regularizer. These ideas are plausible and, according to the ablations, beneficial, especially for unseen attribute types.

The empirical section is generally solid. The paper compares against closed-world tagging baselines, OA-Mine-style open-world baselines, and several internal ablations. The gains are fairly consistent, and the decomposition by seed/new types and title/bullet-point subsets is informative. I especially appreciated Table 4 and Table 5, which reveal that the task remains difficult and that improvements on new attributes are not merely inherited from better performance on seed types. The qualitative examples are also useful, particularly because they show both successes and characteristic failure modes.

That said, I have several concerns that limit my enthusiasm.

The first concern is evaluation clarity and validity. The paper’s main metric is a “pseudo-F1” derived by averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as a proxy for precision and combining that with recall. This is unconventional and somewhat hard to interpret. Jaccard, ARI, and NMI are clustering agreement metrics with different scales and behaviors; averaging them and calling the result “pseudo precision” is not theoretically justified. Because the paper’s headline claims rely on this F1, the evaluation framework needs stronger justification. At minimum, the authors should explain why this aggregation is preferable to reporting the clustering metrics separately, or to using a more standard clustering evaluation protocol for open extraction. As it stands, the main score is somewhat ad hoc.

Relatedly, the evaluation setup mixes span extraction quality and clustering quality in a way that is not always easy to disentangle. The paper does provide a “gold spans as candidates” analysis, which helps, but the main results still depend heavily on candidate generation. Since the syntax-based candidate generator is a major source of gains, it would be useful to know much more about candidate recall and precision by category and by attribute type. Table 5 suggests span extraction remains weak, with exact precision below 34, which means downstream clustering is operating over a noisy candidate pool. This is not a flaw in itself, but it makes it harder to attribute gains specifically to the representation learning innovations.

A second concern is the fairness and strength of the baselines. The paper compares against OA-Mine and some tagging models, but the comparison space still feels somewhat narrow. Since the core of the method is embedding learning plus clustering, stronger modern baselines would be valuable. For example, one would like to see whether a strong sentence/span embedding model with straightforward clustering and nearest-seed assignment could close much of the gap. Similarly, the latent-attribute regularizer should ideally be compared against simpler unsupervised regularizers, such as product-level co-occurrence graph objectives, SimCSE-style augmentations, or even standard topic-model features used post hoc. Without such comparisons, it is difficult to know whether the gains come from the specific proposed formulation or simply from adding any extra weak signal.

A third concern is that some methodological choices are heuristic and under-justified. The self-supervised assumption that spans in the same bullet point are semantically closer than spans in different bullet points of the same product is plausible but noisy. In many product descriptions, a bullet point can mention multiple unrelated attributes, while different bullet points may elaborate on the same attribute. The paper acknowledges noise but does not quantify it. Likewise, the adaptive threshold for seed expansion is based on average intra-seed cosine distance scaled by a global relaxation parameter. This is intuitive, but it is not obvious why this threshold should transfer well across attributes with very different semantic variability. More analysis of threshold sensitivity and failure cases would strengthen confidence in the approach.

The latent-attribute component is interesting, but its contribution is not fully convincing yet. The paper states that it contributes around 70% of the regularization improvement, but the exact ablation details are not visible in the main text. Given that this is arguably the most novel technical contribution, it deserves more direct analysis. For example: how sensitive is performance to the number of latent attributes K? How severe is topic collapse in practice, and how much does it hurt downstream extraction? Are the learned latent attributes category-specific or shared? Does the latent model mainly help by smoothing embeddings, or does it actually induce clusters aligned with unseen attributes? The qualitative examples are suggestive, but more quantitative evidence would help.

The dataset contribution is promising, but I would have liked more detail on annotation quality and reproducibility in the main paper. The test set is annotated by two in-house annotators, but there is no mention here of inter-annotator agreement, adjudication procedure, or detailed annotation guidelines beyond non-overlap and single-label assignment. Since open-world attribute boundaries and type definitions can be subjective, agreement statistics are especially important. The paper also claims 66 attribute types with 42% unseen types from the seed set, but it is not entirely clear how stable these type inventories are across annotators and categories. More transparency here would improve confidence in the benchmark.

There are also some limitations in scope that should be emphasized more clearly. The dataset covers only four categories, all from Amazon, all in English. The method depends on POS tagging quality and on POS patterns extracted from profile values. This may transfer reasonably within English e-commerce, but it is unclear how robust it would be to noisier marketplaces, multilingual settings, or categories with more compositional and relational attributes. The paper argues that the approach is scalable, but the evidence for cross-domain generalization is limited. Even a leave-one-category-out experiment or transfer experiment would have been informative.

Another issue is that the paper’s notion of “new attribute discovery” is cluster discovery without naming. This is acceptable and clearly stated, but it means the system does not fully solve open-world schema induction; it only groups values that may correspond to latent attributes. In practice, downstream applications often need canonical attribute names or mappings to taxonomies. The paper should be more explicit that this is value clustering rather than full attribute induction, and discuss how clusters might be named or validated in deployment.

On the presentation side, the paper is mostly readable, but there are several places where the writing could be tightened. Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially around “practical solution” and “decent coverage.” The mathematical notation is mostly clear, though there are a few inconsistencies and minor imprecisions. For example, the supervised contrastive denominator notation appears unusual relative to standard formulations, and the KL term notation in the latent model could be more precise about whether it is between Gaussian posterior and prior before or after softmax. These are fixable, but they matter for reproducibility.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The problem is important, the dataset appears useful, and the method is a sensible and effective combination of ideas tailored to a realistic weak-supervision regime. The gains on unseen attributes are particularly encouraging, even if the task remains far from solved. I also appreciate that the paper does not hide the difficulty of the setting: the low span-level exact F1 and the qualitative failure cases make clear that this is a challenging benchmark rather than an artificially easy one.

For improvement, I would strongly encourage the authors to do the following. First, strengthen the evaluation section by either replacing the pseudo-F1 with a more principled summary metric or providing a much stronger justification for it. Second, add more baseline comparisons, especially stronger embedding-plus-clustering baselines and simpler weakly supervised regularizers. Third, provide fuller ablations for the latent-attribute and self-supervised components, including sensitivity to K and regularization weights. Fourth, report annotation agreement and more dataset construction details in the main paper. Fifth, include more analysis of candidate generation recall/precision and category-wise behavior, since this stage is central to the overall gains.

In summary, this is a good paper on an important emerging problem. Its main strengths are the realistic task formulation, practical dataset construction, and a coherent lightly supervised method that improves substantially over prior open-world attribute mining baselines. Its main weaknesses are the somewhat ad hoc evaluation summary metric, limited baseline breadth, and insufficient analysis of annotation quality and the most novel latent-attribute component. I would lean positive overall, especially if the venue values practical open-world information extraction and dataset contributions, but I think the paper would benefit from a stronger empirical and evaluative foundation.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper introduces a new lightly supervised open-world product attribute mining setting, where a model must both expand values for known seed attribute types and discover values for previously unseen attribute types without explicit type names. To support this setting, the authors construct the WoaM dataset over four Amazon product categories with seed attributes, a corpus, and a human-annotated test set. They propose Amacer, a pipeline consisting of syntax-based candidate span generation using POS patterns, supervised contrastive representation learning from seed attributes, adaptive expansion for assigning candidates to seed types, DBSCAN for remaining candidates, and two additional regularizers for unseen attributes: a self-supervised bullet-point co-occurrence contrastive loss and an unsupervised latent-attribute topic-model-like objective. Experiments show improvements over OA-Mine and tagging baselines on their proposed clustering-style evaluation, with gains especially on new attribute types.
strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and underexplored setting between closed-world extraction and zero-shot extraction: discovering unseen attribute types under limited supervision.
Creates a new dataset with explicit emphasis on open-world evaluation, including titles and bullet points, which is more realistic than title-only settings.
The overall pipeline is intuitive and modular: candidate generation, representation learning, seed expansion, and clustering are clearly separated.
The syntax-based candidate generation is simple, scalable, and empirically appears stronger than segmentation-based alternatives in this setting.

The use of additional implicit signals for unseen attributes is a meaningful idea; the latent-attribute regularization is a reasonable attempt to inject corpus-level structure beyond seed supervision.
Empirical results show consistent gains over several baselines and include ablations comparing segmentation vs syntax candidates and regularized vs non-regularized variants.
The paper includes useful qualitative analysis and decomposed evaluation on seed vs new attributes and title vs bullet-point text.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is unconventional and somewhat difficult to interpret: the main metric is a pseudo-F1 built from averaging clustering metrics (Jaccard/ARI/NMI) as pseudo-precision and combining with recall, which lacks a strong theoretical justification.
Comparison across model families is not entirely fair because candidate generation differs substantially and appears to dominate performance; some baselines are disadvantaged by design.

The proposed supervised contrastive loss appears to be incorrectly formulated, with the denominator excluding positives and possibly the anchor itself, deviating from standard supervised contrastive learning.
The adaptive expansion thresholding rule is heuristic and may be unstable across attributes with heterogeneous intra-class variance; there is limited analysis of sensitivity or failure modes.
The latent-attribute module is only loosely connected to attribute discovery quality, and the paper itself notes topic collapse; the contribution may be weaker than claimed.
The dataset scope is limited to four categories from a single marketplace and English only, raising concerns about generalization.
Candidate span extraction quality remains low in absolute terms, with span exact F1 below 37, suggesting the end-to-end utility may still be limited despite clustering gains.
The paper does not provide enough annotation-quality details such as inter-annotator agreement, adjudication protocol, or robustness of the notion of 'reasonable attribute values' for new types.
methodological_flaws: The supervised contrastive objective in Eq. for L^su is mathematically inconsistent with the standard supervised contrastive loss. The denominator sums only over negatives N^s(i)=I^s\P^s(i), rather than all non-anchor examples including positives. This changes the optimization behavior substantially and can make the claimed connection to supervised contrastive learning inaccurate.

The self-supervised contrastive loss L^ss repeats the same issue: the denominator uses only negatives from different bullet points, not the standard normalization over all candidate comparisons. This weakens the theoretical grounding of the contrastive formulation.

The notation around cosine distance/similarity is inconsistent. Eq. (1) and Eq. (2) refer to cosine(), but the text alternates between cosine similarity and cosine distance. If cosine similarity is used, the decision rule D(c_i,S_j) < t_j is logically inverted; if cosine distance is used, Eq. (2) based on average within-support 'cosine' is ambiguous. This is a scientific logic issue because the thresholding criterion depends critically on the sign/definition.

The latent-variable formulation is not fully rigorous. The KL term is written as KL(\tilde{\alpha}^p || \hat{\alpha}), but \tilde{\alpha}^p is sampled Gaussian logits before softmax while \hat{\alpha} is described as a standard Gaussian prior Product-to-Attribute distribution; the notation conflates Gaussian latent variables with simplex probabilities. This makes the probabilistic model description imprecise.

The main evaluation metric ('pseudo-F1') is ad hoc and not standard for clustering or extraction. Averaging Jaccard, ARI, and NMI as pseudo-precision and combining with recall lacks clear statistical meaning, so the headline gains may not correspond to a well-defined task objective.

Statistical significance claims are weakly supported: only a t-test at >95% confidence is mentioned, but the unit of testing, number of runs, and variance sources are not clearly specified. With only four categories, significance across macro-averaged scores may be unreliable.

Empirical validity is limited by possible leakage/bias from using product profiles both to derive POS patterns and to construct seed sets, while evaluation is on related products from the same marketplace/categories. This may overstate generalization to truly novel domains or attribute expressions.
